Isosceles Triangle In Circle

TrianglesCirclesConstructions
Game: Move the corners of a triangle and watch a line from its middle point to the centre of the circle through all three corners.
How to play: Drag A, B or C with a mouse or finger, or focus a dot and use the arrow keys. Toggle the names, premise and hint, then press Check the claim.
Look for the math

D is the midpoint of AB and E is the centroid of triangle ACD. O is the circumcenter of ABC. The claim is that the line EO is at right angles to CD exactly when the two sides AB and AC are equal. Drag the corners: the green line turns with the triangle, and the right angle appears only at that special shape.

Turn lengths into a dot product

Put the origin at O, so A·A = B·B = C·C for all three corners on the circumcircle. Then D = (A + B)/2 and E = (A + D + C)/3 = (3A + 2C + B)/6. Expanding the dot product of EO with CD gives a short identity:

(E − O)·(D − C) = (1/3) A·(B − C) = (AC² − AB²)/6.

That product is zero exactly when AC² = AB², which means AB = AC. So EO is perpendicular to CD exactly when the triangle is isosceles at A. The same identity is zero exactly when AO is perpendicular to BC, so all three conditions agree.

Where the right angle comes from

Press Show premise to see the circle and the marks: D splits AB in half, F splits AC in half, and the point called Am splits CD in half. Line DF is parallel to BC, and line PE is parallel to AB. When AB = AC, the median AM is also an altitude, so P and O both lie on AM. In triangle PDE the point O is the orthocenter: DO is perpendicular to PE and PO is perpendicular to DE. The third altitude from E must then be perpendicular to DP, which is CD. Press Show hint to see that right angle, the helper points S, M and P, and the median from A.

What was checked

The page's "if and only if" claim holds for every triangle with a circumcenter. The logic test checks the identity and the claim on all 4,096 triangles of a lattice, on more than a thousand random triangles, and on 240 exact isosceles triangles; it also checks the reverse direction on scalene triangles. A second transcription of the applet's own Midpoint, Average, FindCircumcenter, NearestPoint and CheckFinished methods agrees on every case. If A, B and C lie in one line there is no circumcircle and the port says the claim is undefined. The applet's "Finished" eye lights up when |AB − AC| < 1 screen pixel, which is a drawing tolerance, not mathematical equality.

Try putting A directly above the midpoint of BC: AB and AC match and the green line meets CD at a right angle.
